summary: Future habitats on the Moon and Mars will run at lower pressure and higher oxygen than the ISS, and fire behaves differently there. NASA has flown many combustion experiments, but their results are spread across the Physical Science Informatics (PSI) system, technical reports and papers, each at different conditions. EMBER turns them into one evidence registry of 982 records from 11 NASA investigations and 19 cited sources. A designer enters an atmosphere; EMBER ranks every experiment by a transfer distance D, built from NASA's published flame-spread scaling exponents (Ruff 2021), so you can see both which tests apply and how far you are extrapolating. A gap map shows conditions no one has tested. EMBER never fills in unknown values, never calls an atmosphere safe, and treats Moon and Mars gravity as a bracket between microgravity and 1-g tests, because PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data. It runs fully offline.
details:
Live App: https://9a8sdjcy2q4hvryba8dpp7.streamlit.app/

What it does. You describe a habitat atmosphere (oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity, material) or ask a question in plain English. EMBER shows which NASA fire experiments apply, ranks them, says how far each one is from your conditions, and maps what has never been tested.

How it works.

  • Evidence registry. Every PSI combustion record is placed in oxygen–pressure–flow space with its gravity, fuel and phenomenon. Every value traces to a table row or a page in a cited source. Values from papers enter only after a named human reviewer accepts them.
  • Transfer distance D. An elasticity-weighted log distance whose weights are NASA's published flame-spread exponents (Ruff 2021), so exp(D) reads as "how much the flame-spread response could differ". D > 1 is flagged as beyond the tested envelope. Missing conditions make D a lower bound instead of being imputed. Gravity is a flag, never interpolated.
  • Gap map. Coverage per gravity regime, plotted against NASA's target exploration atmospheres (NASA-TP-2010-216134), with an exportable gap report.
  • Compare. Rule gates (gravity, fuel, flow, hardware, granularity) list every confounder before saying whether two results can be compared.
  • Honesty rules. CFI-G's 85% O₂ is labelled burner-side oxidizer flow, never a cabin atmosphere. LUCI's simulated lunar gravity is labelled non-PSI. Nothing is called "safe".

What we measured.

  • Rank stability: in both demo scenarios (lunar habitat at 34% O₂ and 56.5 kPa / 8.2 psi, and Earth air), all of the top 5 stay in the top 5 in at least 80% of 1,000 re-rankings with every weight perturbed (elasticities ±30%, priors ±50%).
  • Trick prompts: 5 of 5 handled ("Is Nomex safe at 34% O₂?" is refused; "What did FLEX measure on the Moon?" is flagged as a partial-gravity question).
  • Hostile sentences: 8 of 8 dropped by the cite-or-drop verifier.
  • Compare rules: 0 false "comparable" verdicts on 12 starter pairs (a smoke test, not a rate).
  • Data integrity: 29 of 47 listed NASA files mirrored locally and SHA-256 verified.
  • Not yet measured: the retrieval benchmark (40 questions, five baselines) is built, but it needs two human relevance labellers before it reports a score. We show it as pending rather than grade ourselves.

Benefits. A habitat or materials engineer gets, in one screen, the experiments that bear on their atmosphere, an honest measure of extrapolation, and a list of what has not been tested. That saves days of searching PSI and NTRS, and it makes the gaps visible instead of hidden behind a confident-looking answer.

What we hope to achieve. Point the next round of spacecraft fire experiments at the untested conditions that matter for Artemis and Mars habitats: lunar and Mars gravity at the exploration atmospheres NASA is considering. Next steps are human relevance labels for the benchmark, more reviewed NTRS papers, and partial-gravity data from LUCI and FM2 as it is published.

Tools, languages, hardware and software. Python 3.12; Streamlit (interface); Plotly (charts); pandas, NumPy, SciPy; pydantic (schemas); pint (units); DuckDB and Parquet/pyarrow (storage); pdfplumber (PDF tables); httpx (downloads); rank_bm25, sentence-transformers and FAISS (benchmark baselines); pytest (216 tests) and ruff; uv (environments). Optional Anthropic Claude API for question parsing and cited summaries; without it a rule-based parser and template summaries run through the same verifier. Runs offline on a laptop; no special hardware.

NASA Data

  • NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) investigation records and data tables: BASS (PSI-26), BASS-II (PSI-25), Saffire-I (PSI-98), Saffire-III (PSI-100), ACME CFI-G (PSI-159), FLEX (PSI-69), SAME (PSI-102), SAME-R (PSI-101), DAFT / DAFT-2 (PSI-47). https://psi.ndc.nasa.gov
  • NASA Technical Reports Server (https://ntrs.nasa.gov): Saffire VI preliminary results (20240002981); LUCI simulated lunar gravity burns (20250010653); Flammability of Materials on the Moon, FM2 (20240015307); Ruff, Technology Development for Spacecraft Fire Safety (20210021318).
  • NASA-TP-2010-216134, Recommendations for Exploration Spacecraft Internal Atmospheres.
  • NASA DAFT fact sheet (2025).

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

Other references (peer-reviewed papers cited in the registry). Link et al. 2018, Scientific Reports, 10.1038/s41598-017-18398-4; Nayagam et al. 2014, Microgravity Science and Technology, 10.1007/s12217-014-9372-2; Meyer et al., PMC7918997.

Software (all open source). Python, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pydantic, pint, DuckDB, pyarrow, pdfplumber, httpx, PyYAML, rank_bm25, sentence-transformers, FAISS, pytest, ruff, uv. Optional: Anthropic Python SDK.

Fonts. Libre Caslon Text, Libre Caslon Display and Libre Franklin (SIL Open Font License), bundled in app/static/fonts so the app works offline.

AI tools. Anthropic Claude (Claude Code) as a coding assistant; see Use of SI.
